actual_action: New South Wales enacted the Aborigines Protection Amending Act 1915. The amendment removed the prior requirement that the Board first establish neglect in court and empowered it, after its own due inquiry, to assume full control and custody of an Aboriginal child when it considered that course to be in the child's moral or physical welfare. Parents could appeal after removal.
later_evidence: The National Inquiry later reconstructed that from 1915 until 1940 the NSW Aborigines Protection Board could remove Aboriginal children under this special Board-centred power without the initial court neglect finding required under the earlier framework.

The National Inquiry documented that forced-removal policies across Australia separated children from parents, siblings, communities, culture and Country and that many children experienced institutionalisation, exploitation, abuse, denigration of Aboriginal identity and barriers to family contact.

Later evidence showed significant family, cultural, psychological and intergenerational harms associated with forcible separation, while experiences and outcomes varied between individuals and placements.

The 1940 NSW legislative changes removed the Protection Board's special direct removal power; Aboriginal child removals thereafter operated through the general child-welfare legal framework, although removals and institutional placements continued.
outcomes: The 1915 change materially shifted coercive child-removal authority from a prior judicial neglect process to an ancestry-specific administrative Board determination followed by a parental right of appeal.

The power formed part of the NSW legal and administrative machinery under which Aboriginal children were separated from families and placed in institutions, apprenticeships or other care arrangements.
The later National Inquiry found that forcible-removal laws, policies and practices produced serious harms not only for many removed children but also for families, communities and later generations.
later_reviews_or_findings: The 1997 Bringing Them Home National Inquiry traced the NSW 1915 amendment as a key child-removal law and explicitly contrasted such special powers with ordinary legal protections applying to non-Indigenous families.

The Inquiry emphasised that historical government conduct should not be judged as though the past had only today's values; it also found that dissenting views existed at the time and that there was never universal agreement that such policies were right or just.
Bringing Them Home recommended acknowledgment, apology, guarantees against repetition, restitution, rehabilitation and monetary compensation as components of reparation for forcible-removal harms.
